The soldier was with a volunteer regiment from Vermont, as I recall, one of the first to actively participate in the war effort. Vermont regiments, like all regiments at that time, were very closely knit in an unfamiliar place, far from home. Nobody really knows why he fell asleep. Covering for a sick comrade was one thought. Others suggest that most of the northern recruits were subject to dysentery from the swampy marshlands that surrounded the capital. When you don't feel well, you sleep a lot. But then the story gets muddied by all the attention it brought about. It was the first propaganda story from the war, similar to a later story from the Iraq war, and drummed up support for the war during the very beginning of the conflict. There was a long poem written about the soldier's case that was published and recited at events and public gatherings. Most people were very critical of executing him. They brought him out that morning and had selected a group of four to fire at him. They pinned a white circle of cloth on his blouse, and three were given blanks while one had a live round. At the last moment, the pardon issued by the President was read, and he was released. The following spring, he took part in a failed military campaign and was killed while carrying another soldier away from a futile attempt to rush a fortified position surrounded by a swamp.
